Here are practical things to check when you try guitars at the music store this weekend, based on what we discussed earlier about Strat vs Les Paul, pickup options, and setup for alternate tunings:

- Body & construction: compare a Strat-style (lighter, contoured, bolt-on) vs a Les Paul–style (heavier, set neck, mahogany/maple) to see which weight and feel you prefer.
- Neck shape & playability: play up and down the neck to judge the profile, fretboard radius, and how comfortable chord shapes and single-note lines feel.
- Pickups & tone options: try single-coils and humbuckers to hear the difference (single-coils are brighter/cleaner; humbuckers are warmer/thicker). If a guitar has coil-tap/coil-splitting, try those settings to hear extra tonal flexibility.
- Sustain & resonance: play long notes and bends to judge sustain (Les Paul–style guitars tend to have more sustain and a thicker tone).
- Setup and action: check string height and intonation—low action makes playing easier but can fret out; ask if the shop can adjust the setup or show you how it plays with different string gauges.
- Strings & tuning: if you plan to use alternate tunings (you mentioned open D), try the guitar with a heavier string set and/or ask about how it feels in that tuning—heavier strings can give a fuller tone in lower tunings.
- Electronics & hardware: test pots, switches, and the pickup selector for any crackling or noise. Check the tuners for stability and the bridge for height/adjustability.
- Amp and effects: play the guitar through an amp and through any pedals you use to get a realistic idea of its sound in the rig you’ll use.
- Play your songs: bring a short set of things you know (chords, riffs, any fingerpicking passages you want to play) so you can judge how the guitar handles the styles you play—including any acoustic-like fingerpicking you care about.
- Comfort & finish: sit and stand with the guitar for a few minutes to judge strap balance, finish feel, and overall comfort.

If you want, tell me which models you’ll try (Strat, Les Paul, specific brands/models) and I can highlight likely tonal and setup differences to listen for.

Based on what you told me earlier (you already back up to an external drive, want a central backup for laptop and phone, are a beginner, and are concerned about security), I’d lean toward buying a NAS now if you need the convenience and extra storage today. A NAS will let you centralize backups (Time Machine/Windows backup and phone backups), make scheduled automatic backups, and give you more capacity than a single external drive.

Practical guidance from our prior discussion to help pick one now:
- If you’re a beginner and want something easy to set up, a compact 2‑bay model is often the right start (more affordable and simpler). We specifically talked about Synology’s DS218j as a good, beginner‑friendly option. 
- If you anticipate needing lots of expansion or redundancy beyond basic mirroring, consider a 4‑bay (or larger) so you can add drives or use more advanced RAID later. 
- Prioritize security features you asked about: at-rest encryption, access controls/ACLs, and two‑factor authentication. We discussed that higher‑end models (e.g., Synology DiskStation models like the DS1819+ mentioned) expose AES encryption, granular permissions, and 2FA support.

When you might wait:
- If you don’t urgently need extra storage or automated backups right now, waiting lets you research deals, compare models, or decide whether 2‑bay vs 4‑bay fits your long‑term needs.

Bottom line: If centralizing backups and improving convenience/security is a current need, buy a beginner‑friendly 2‑bay NAS now (Synology DS218j or similar) and make sure it supports encryption, ACLs, and 2FA. If you don’t need it immediately, waiting to clarify future capacity needs or hunt for deals is reasonable.
